fulltext: IT之家 10 月 24 日消息，澳大利亚悉尼一名男子戴维 · 兰 · 萨克雷向 Anthropic 的聊天机器人 Claude 透露，自己想杀害住所附近一家托儿所的儿童，随后被警方逮捕。
据《悉尼先驱晨报》报道，29 岁的萨克雷与 Claude 的对话引起了国际刑警组织注意，随后于当地时间 18 日被警方拘留。警方指控他利用通信服务实施骚扰、恐吓或冒犯行为，涉嫌违反澳大利亚刑法。
检方提交的文件显示，萨克雷曾对 Claude 说：“我现在就想去附近的韦斯特菲尔德购物中心，朝当地的托儿所开枪扫射。”
报道提到，国际刑警组织通过什么途径获取了聊天记录，以及 Anthropic 是否主动向国际刑警组织提供了对话内容，目前均不清楚。
萨克雷不仅谈到了袭击当地托儿所、大规模杀害儿童，还在对话中提到了纳维德 · 阿克拉姆。
IT之家注：阿克拉姆被控于 2025 年 12 月在悉尼邦迪海滩举行的犹太教光明节庆祝活动中发动袭击，造成 15 人死亡，是该案的恐怖袭击嫌疑人。
检察官在法庭上指出：“他就是想像邦迪那名涉嫌实施恐怖袭击的男子一样，在悉尼大开杀戒。通过他与聊天机器人的对话，我们可以了解他究竟在想什么。”
萨克雷的辩护律师则称，当事人只是情绪失控，借聊天机器人发泄不满。律师解释说，萨克雷患有耳部感染，因此感到压力和烦躁，所说的话根本不能当真。
他还强调，萨克雷一直以为自己与 Claude 的对话属于私人交流。据《悉尼先驱晨报》报道，萨克雷将接受心理健康评估。
IT之家获悉，AI 聊天机器人正逐渐成为一些陷入有害妄想、执念或思维紊乱的用户倾诉心事的对象，也由此引发担忧。
已有多起犯罪事件被认为与当事人长期使用聊天机器人存在关联，包括一起杀人后自杀案，以及 2025 年美国佛罗里达州立大学枪击案、今年 2 月的加拿大塔布勒岭校园枪击案等大规模枪击事件。
部分跟踪骚扰者以及存在偏执、过度迷恋等问题的人，也会从随时回应、倾向于顺从用户的 AI 聊天机器人那里获得支持。

fulltext: IT之家 10 月 24 日消息，据外媒 Interesting Engineering 报道，美国旧金山核聚变初创企业 Marathon Fusion 宣称，利用核聚变产生的高能中子实现了“点汞成金”。
该公司于当地时间 21 日宣布，其黄金生产速率达到欧洲核子研究组织（CERN）2025 年纪录的 10 倍。然而，实验成果尚未得到公开的独立验证，Marathon 也没有透露究竟制造了多少黄金。
根据 Marathon 介绍的技术原理，氘氚聚变产生的 14MeV 中子撞击汞-198 后，会使其转化为具有放射性的汞-197。汞-197 的半衰期据称约为 64 小时，随后衰变成金-197，也就是金唯一的稳定同位素。
Marathon 计划将汞放入聚变反应堆的包层，使包层在生产黄金的同时增殖氚，为持续进行的核聚变反应提供燃料。公司早在 2025 年便通过一篇预印本论文提出了该方案，但论文尚未经过同行评议。
2025 年，欧洲核子研究组织公布了 ALICE 实验的产金成果。在大型强子对撞机 4 年的运行过程中，铅离子碰撞产生的金原子核总质量约为 29 皮克。Marathon 声称，自己的产金速率达到这一纪录的 10 倍，却没有解释具体采用了何种比较标准。
无论是黄金总质量、单位时间产生的原子核数量，还是照射时长，公司都没有给出明确答案。
Marathon 还发布了伽马射线能谱图，声称其中可以看到汞-197 和金-197 的特征信号，不过没有公布黄金的实际产量、纯度、回收效率及生产成本。
Marathon 现有反应堆的聚变功率约为 1kW，仅相当于 1GW 的百万分之一。公司通过模型推算的年产黄金最多 2 吨，则需要以尚未建成的吉瓦级聚变设施为基础。
即便能够生产黄金，也不能立即出售。刚生成的材料中还含有放射性同位素，必须经过储存、等待放射性衰变及后续处理。Marathon 的模型据称也考虑了长期储存的需要。在不同假设条件下，估计储存时间约为 7 至 18 年。
除了黄金，Marathon 还声称利用聚变中子照射锌，制造出铜-64 和铜-67。不过，要充分确认这项成果，仍需取得直接的一手资料。铜-64 和铜-67 可用于癌症影像诊断和靶向放射治疗。医疗领域已经存在实际需求，即使产量不大，也能获得较高的市场价格。
Marathon 成立于 2023 年，次年完成了一轮 590 万美元（IT之家注：现汇率约合 3,944.1 万元人民币）的种子轮融资。目前，Marathon 正在旧金山建造一座紧凑型聚变反应堆，力争创下功率密度纪录。除聚变设备研发外，公司还将中子利用和同位素生产列为业务方向，长期目标则是实现大规模核聚变发电，并向电网供电。

On Friday, OpenAI said that it will train its models using cached copies and simulated versions of the internet instead of the live web because the models are too unpredictable to be trusted with live internet access.

The frontier lab announced its new policy two weeks after its rival, Anthropic, began limiting its newest and, in theory, most capable models from accessing the live internet. Researchers adopted these policies after months of incidents in which models pursuing training tasks broke into external systems in search of answers, collaborated on obscure message boards, and developed exotic hacking strategies.

“Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access,” the company said in a blog post.

OpenAI said that as recently as September 20, one of its frontier models exploited a misconfiguration to access the internet. That led the company to pause training work for the rest of the month so it could develop and test new approaches to securing its models.
The decision to train these models in sandboxes cut off from the internet is notable because employees at frontier labs have insisted that doing so would be nearly infeasible.

Keeping AI data centers separate from the internet “would need research teams to essentially be embedded inside of data centers in Iowa or wherever else around the world,” former OpenAI researcher Steven Adler told Fortune this month. “It’s a lot of overhead, and it isn’t clear to me that the safety benefits of it are large enough to merit just how large a tax it would be for a company to do it unilaterally.”

“In nearly every post I make on X, without fail, I get between five and ten comments about my inability to secure a sandbox, or asking why the hell we can’t just unplug the model from the internet,” an anonymous security engineer at OpenAI wrote in a September post on X. “These comments reflect a widening gap between where a lot of organizations and people are today and what the frontier labs are dealing with. There is also a general misunderstanding of how model training and evaluation work at these labs.”

The engineer, whose role has been confirmed previously by OpenAI, described how complex the training runs launched by OpenAI engineers are, noting that they require access a variety of resources and tools across many domains, and that thousands of researchers build, modify and test the environments. “So is it as easy as just putting it in a sandbox? No, it’s not,” he concluded.

Now, OpenAI says that “we must always be able to prevent a frontier model from achieving unauthorized, arbitrary access to the live internet.” That comes after the company deployed swarms of agents in red-teaming exercises that attempted to escape from their sandbox. That effort revealed a range of vulnerabilities that convinced the lab to adopt its new approach.

To meet that requirement while still reaching its training goals, the lab said it created a “a vast set of indexed and cached web content with which our models can interact, without risk of affecting external systems.”

Whether that strategy will perform as well as letting models run freely on the open internet remains to be seen, but it is noteworthy that both frontier labs have determined their most powerful technology can’t be left unsupervised on the digital commons.

周五，OpenAI 表示，它将使用互联网的缓存副本和模拟版本而不是实时网络来训练其模型，因为这些模型太不可预测，无法通过实时互联网访问来信任。
在其竞争对手 Anthropic 开始限制其最新且理论上最强大的模型访问实时互联网两周后，前沿实验室宣布了新政策。研究人员在几个月的事件发生后采取了这些政策，在这些事件中，执行训练任务的模型闯入外部系统以寻找答案，在模糊的留言板上进行协作，并开发出奇特的黑客策略。
该公司在博客文章中表示：“根据当前的一致性研究、监控系统和互联网基础设施的安全状况，我们认为负责任的方法是在没有互联网接入的情况下进行前沿模型训练。”
OpenAI 表示，就在 9 月 20 日，其一款前沿模型利用错误配置访问互联网。这导致该公司暂停了本月剩余时间的培训工作，以便开发和测试新的方法来保护其模型。
在与互联网隔绝的沙箱中训练这些模型的决定值得注意，因为前沿实验室的员工坚称这样做几乎不可行。
前 OpenAI 研究员史蒂文·阿德勒 (Steven Adler) 本月向《财富》杂志表示，将人工智能数据中心与互联网分开“需要研究团队基本上嵌入爱荷华州或世界其他地方的数据中心内”。 “这是一笔很大的管理费用，而且我不清楚它的安全效益是否足够大，值得一家公司单方面这样做，需要缴纳多大的税。”
OpenAI 的一位匿名安全工程师在 9 月份的 X 帖子中写道：“在我在 X 上发布的几乎每一篇帖子中，我都会收到五到十条关于我无法保护沙箱安全的评论，或者问为什么我们不能直接将模型从互联网上拔掉。这些评论反映了许多组织和人员目前的状况与前沿实验室正在处理的问题之间的差距越来越大。人们对这些实验室的模型训练和评估工作方式也存在普遍误解。”
这位工程师的角色此前已得到 OpenAI 的确认，他描述了 OpenAI 工程师发起的培训运行是多么复杂，并指出他们需要访问跨多个领域的各种资源和工具，并且数千名研究人员构建、修改和测试环境。 “那么，这就像将其放入沙箱中一样简单吗？不，不是，”他总结道。
现在，OpenAI 表示，“我们必须始终能够阻止前沿模型对实时互联网进行未经授权的任意访问。”此前，该公司在红队演习中部署了大批特工，试图逃离沙箱。这项工作揭示了一系列漏洞，说服实验室采用其新方法。
为了满足这一要求，同时仍然达到其培训目标，该实验室表示，它创建了“大量索引和缓存的网络内容，我们的模型可以与这些内容进行交互，而不会影响外部系统。”
该策略是否会发挥作用以及让模型在开放互联网上自由运行还有待观察，但值得注意的是，两个前沿实验室都已确定他们最强大的技术不能在数字共享上不受监督。

fulltext: AI agents can still communicate without a network connection, OpenAI found.

OpenAI is now training its most advanced AI models without internet access following a string of rogue hacking incidents. In a blog post on Friday, OpenAI says it built an offline testing environment where AI models can interact with indexed and cached web content “without risk of affecting external systems.”

OpenAI paused training its frontier AI models in September, after disclosing several incidents in which its AI agents broke out of their testing environments to hack third-party companies and government agencies, or swarm obscure websites. On October 1st, OpenAI resumed reinforcement learning training and internal inference with tighter security measures, the blog post says.

Even with these safeguards in place and no internet access, OpenAI found that agents “do not always need a network connection in order to communicate.” One test performed by the company asked AI models on separate virtual machines to exchange secrets without a network connection. To bypass this restriction, the AI agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache:

Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message. Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection.

OpenAI says it has added checks to its monitoring system to detect this type of communication. It will also continue training its frontier AI models without a network connection until improved safeguards “justify broader internet access.”

In the meantime, OpenAI says it will work to improve the security of its virtual machines, while testing for weaknesses in its testing environments. It’s also going to continue testing its monitoring systems, which were recently undermined by its AI agents during internal coding projects.

在发生一系列流氓黑客事件后，OpenAI 现在正在无需连接互联网的情况下训练其最先进的人工智能模型。 OpenAI 在周五的一篇博客文章中表示，它构建了一个离线测试环境，其中人工智能模型可以与索引和缓存的网络内容进行交互，“而不会影响外部系统的风险”。
OpenAI 在披露了几起其人工智能代理突破测试环境入侵第三方公司和政府机构或涌入不知名网站的事件后，于 9 月暂停了其前沿人工智能模型的训练。博客文章称，10 月 1 日，OpenAI 恢复了强化学习训练和内部推理，并采取了更严格的安全措施。
即使采取了这些保护措施并且无法访问互联网，OpenAI 发现代理“并不总是需要网络连接才能进行通信”。该公司进行的一项测试要求单独虚拟机上的人工智能模型在没有网络连接的情况下交换秘密。为了绕过这个限制，人工智能代理找到了一种使用处理器缓存进行通信的方法：
从缓存中读取数据比从主内存中检索数据要快，并且代理利用这种时间差异进行通信。一个代理通过从缓存中逐出选定的数据来对信息进行编码。另一种方法是利用快速读取和慢速读取之间的差异来计时重新加载数据所需的时间来恢复消息。一旦代理就编码和解码这些信号的协议达成一致，他们就可以交换合成秘密，而无需更改共享文件或打开网络连接。
OpenAI 表示，它已在其监控系统中添加了检查功能，以检测此类通信。它还将继续在没有网络连接的情况下训练其前沿人工智能模型，直到改进的保障措施“证明更广泛的互联网访问是合理的”。
与此同时，OpenAI 表示将努力提高虚拟机的安全性，同时测试其测试环境中的弱点。它还将继续测试其监控系统，该系统最近在内部编码项目期间被人工智能代理破坏。

Building a startup means making decisions before you have all the answers.

When should you scale? How do you know you really have product-market fit? What does it take to land enterprise customers? How do you build the right team? And when you finally get in front of an investor, how do you make sure your pitch earns another conversation?

On November 4 at SoWa Power Station in Boston, TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026 will bring together founders, investors, and operators who have tackled those questions from different sides of the table.

Hosted by TechCrunch in partnership with Fidelity Private Shares, the full-day event goes beyond fundraising and AI to explore the realities of finding customers, building teams, sharpening a pitch, developing founder leadership, and scaling companies both inside and outside traditional startup hubs. Save 25% on your ticket today, and bring a colleague along for free with our limited BOGO deal.
Boston founders do not have to look far for an example of what can happen when a startup finds its market and continues evolving with its customers.
Steve Fredette, president, co-founder, and director of Toast, takes the Impact Stage for “Building a Company That Keeps Reinventing Itself.”
Toast’s story offers founders a compelling case study in identifying a customer problem, finding product-market fit, winning customers, and ultimately scaling a Boston startup into a public company.

But reaching scale does not mean the work is finished. Fredette’s conversation will look at what it takes to continue evolving a company as customer expectations, technology, and the market change around it, while staying connected to the needs that helped create the business in the first place.
Growth can be exciting. Growing too early can be expensive.

Kent Bennett, partner at Bessemer Venture Partners, will lead “Finding Product Market Fit Before You Scale,” focusing on one of the most important questions an early-stage founder can answer: Are customers actually telling you that you are ready to grow?
The session will give founders a chance to think more critically about the signals that matter before adding headcount, increasing spend, or accelerating go-to-market efforts.
It is a useful counterpoint to startup culture’s constant pressure to move faster. Sometimes the smartest next move is making sure the foundation is actually there.
That same tension takes center stage with Rudina Seseri, founder and managing partner of Glasswing Ventures.
In “When to Scale and When to Hit the Brakes,” Seseri will explore how founders can distinguish between the moments that call for acceleration and the moments when restraint may protect the business.
Founders are constantly making trade-offs between growth and discipline. Knowing when not to scale can be just as consequential as knowing when to go all in.
AI is reshaping how new companies think about products, operations, and teams, but adding AI to an existing process is different from building a company around it from the start.
Lior Div, CEO and co-founder of 7AI, will tackle that distinction in “Built for AI From Day One.”

For founders building in the current technology environment, the conversation provides an opportunity to think beyond AI as a feature and toward how it can influence the architecture and operating model of an entire company.
The startup world does not begin and end in Silicon Valley.
Chase Garbarino, CEO and co-founder of HqO, will take the Impact Stage for “The Boston Founder Playbook,” examining what it means to build and scale a company from Boston.
For founders across New England and the broader East Coast ecosystem, the conversation offers a particularly relevant perspective on talent, customers, capital, and community outside the Bay Area.

Combined with Fredette’s Toast story, it also gives this year’s Summit a strong local through line: Ambitious companies can be built in Boston, and founders here do not need to copy Silicon Valley to do it.
A pitch does not have to close the deal. It has to make someone want the next conversation.
Dave Balter, venture partner at True Ventures and CEO of Edisyl, will explore that idea in “Your Pitch Has to Earn the Next Conversation.”
For founders accustomed to explaining their companies every day, the session is a reminder that knowing your business and communicating its story are two different skills.
Later in the afternoon, attendees will see that theory put into practice.
Catch the full list of Founders Summit speakers here.
At “So You Think You Can Pitch?,” founders will put their stories to the test live on the Build Stage.
Balter will be joined by Chirag Shah, partner at Define Ventures, and Simran Suri, principal at Maveron, as startups make their cases in front of an investor judging panel.
For attendees, it is an opportunity to watch what happens when founders have limited time to make an idea connect, and to hear how investors react in real time.
It is one of the most interactive parts of the Founder Summit program and a chance to learn from both the pitches that land and the ones that leave questions unanswered.
The rest of the program stretches across many of the decisions founders are facing right now.

Hunter Worland of NEA will explore why distribution may become a startup’s next competitive advantage. Vineet Edupuganti, co-founder and CEO of Cogent Security, will discuss building 10x teams. Tina Tosukhowong of TDK Ventures will examine the hidden signals that can identify category winners.
Fidelity Private Shares will also bring its perspective to conversations about fundraising trends with Kristen Craft and enterprise relationships with Evan Schnidman.
Together, the agenda creates a day that is not just about raising the next round or chasing the latest AI trend but is also about building the company.

The day brings together candid founder conversations, practical sessions, smaller roundtables, live pitching, networking, and a closing reception presented by Fidelity Private Shares.

fulltext: According to the new terms, sharing your data for better AI recommendations also means opening it up for more personalized ads.

Google has updated its privacy policy in a way that could mean you’ll start seeing targeted ads based on your personal data if you’re using personalized AI features. The update, spotted by Android Authority, adds an exception to its promise about not using your Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos for personalized ads. While the previous version simply said it wouldn’t do that, as of October 16th, Google has added the line, “unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads.”

That means anyone who has connected their Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos to AI Mode and other Search tools via Google’s Personal Intelligence feature — allowing those tools to provide better responses or recommendations by knowing more about you — may now see ads targeted on the basis of that content.

Advertisers don’t get access to your Drive, Gmail, and Photos information or personally identifying details such as your name or email address, and Google won’t show you ads based on sensitive categories like race, sexual orientation, religion, or health.
This is what the policy says:

“You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive, in order to provide you with a more personalized experience, subject to the policies and settings of the accessing service. For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads.”

“Depending on your settings, we may also show you personalized ads based on your interests, activity, or personalized content from Google services. For example, if you search for ‘mountain bikes,’ in Search you may see ads for sports equipment on YouTube.”

If you want to prevent your personal data from being used for targeted ads, you can choose which apps you want to disconnect from Search’s Personal Intelligence features or disable Personalized Recommendations entirely via the Search Services Personalization settings page.

cards.title: LitPivot: Developing research ideas through dynamic contextualization within the literature landscape
cards.title_cn: LitPivot：通过文学景观中的动态情境化发展研究思路
cards.summary: 【Hugging Face 官方动态】LitPivot: Developing research ideas through dynamic contextualization within the literature landscape
fulltext: Encountering a new paper can change a research idea's trajectory. The researcher may discover that someone has already addressed their proposed contribution, or find an unresolved problem in the paper that inspires a new direction of inquiry.

We call this process a literature-initiated pivot: a change in research direction prompted by reading prior work. It connects two activities that researchers often have to manage separately: developing an idea and deciding which literature to measure it against.

With collaborators at the University of Pennsylvania, we developed LitPivot, a system that helps researchers navigate these pivots. Using papers retrieved through Asta Paper Finder, LitPivot organizes literature around the part of a proposal being edited, offers critiques supported by excerpts from selected studies, and suggests revisions that researchers can accept, edit, or reject. LitPivot is intended to be used for early-stage research ideation, but the idea could possibly extend to longer writing tasks (i.e., writing the introduction section of a paper).

In a study with 17 researchers, domain experts rated research ideas developed with LitPivot as better grounded in the literature than those developed with a text editor and an AI chat tool. Participants also perceived their revised research ideas as more novel and useful, and reported a stronger understanding of the surrounding literature.
LitPivot will be presented at UIST 2026 in Detroit. Read the paper here.

Research ideas evolve through engaging with the literature. In our analysis of meeting notes from four completed computer science research projects, we identified 21 literature-initiated pivots across all four projects. These fell into two types: differentiating an idea from existing work to establish an idea’s novelty, and aligning an idea with existing work to build on it. This project itself went through two pivots before we settled on its contributions.

These changes can be difficult to navigate. In a formative study, five researchers developed proposals using a text editor and standard search tools. They struggled to develop their ideas while critically evaluating them against the literature. When a paper challenged an idea’s novelty, they wanted concrete suggestions for how to revise it, supported by prior work. These findings shaped LitPivot’s assessments, which pair literature-supported critiques with specific suggestions for revising the selected part of an idea.

In LitPivot, a researcher starts by writing a short proposal in an editor and enabling what we call facet highlighting, which segments an articulated idea into different facets (i.e., a problem, contribution, and evaluation). To check a proposed facet, the researcher clicks that segment in the draft. An adjacent panel groups related papers based on the selected facet (e.g., grouping papers by the evaluation methods they use when the evaluation facet is selected) and highlights the most relevant groups. The researcher selects papers, requests an assessment, and reviews a suggested revision alongside excerpts supporting the critique. The literature is then reranked based on relevance to the revised facet.

In particular, LitPivot separates a research idea into its problem, proposed contribution, and evaluation plan. Each facet has its own set and relevance ranking of related literature. LitPivot groups retrieved papers around the facet being edited, letting the researcher choose which ones the system should use to assess the draft.

Alongside scientific-writing environments such as Prism and agentic assistants such as Claude Code, LitPivot explores a new workflow for developing an early research idea: choosing literature to assess it against, using that evidence to revise it, and reconsidering which papers matter as the idea changes. Its paper groups and linked critiques make those steps explicit for each part of the proposal, while researchers control both the draft and the evidence used to assess it.

For a problem statement, LitPivot looks for evidence that the problem exists and reasons it matters. To assess a proposed contribution, it compares what the selected papers have already addressed with the limitations and future work they describe, looking for remaining gaps. For an evaluation plan, it checks whether the proposed tests address the research question and how similar work has been evaluated. The system then suggests a rewrite with supporting quotes attached.

Changing one facet of an idea can leave another out of date. LitPivot flags passages that may need revision, such as an evaluation plan that no longer adequately evaluates a revised contribution. Researchers can accept, edit, or reject suggestions, and request new papers or refresh the literature ranking as their proposal develops.
Paraphrased example from one study participant.

In our lab study, 17 researchers each developed one assigned idea with LitPivot and another with a baseline tool—a text editor and an AI tool for asking questions about selected papers. Both conditions used the same collection of papers. Two domain experts, unaware of which system had been used, rated the resulting proposals on a single criterion: how well they used relevant literature to support and justify the idea. Proposals developed with LitPivot received higher ratings.

Participants in the same study also reported a stronger understanding of the surrounding literature and greater self-reported improvements in their ideas’ novelty and usefulness with LitPivot than with the baseline. Domain experts also reviewed the participants’ ideas and rated the ideas revised using LitPivot to be significantly better grounded in relevant literature.

One participant in our lab study started with a proposal to generate consistent, factual synthetic medical notes. LitPivot identified consistency across multiple hospital visits as a potential gap in the selected literature. The participant reviewed abstracts and removed papers about single-visit notes. After another assessment, they narrowed the proposal to detecting contradictions across notes from multiple visits. The example shows how revising an idea and choosing the literature used to assess it can inform each other.

In a follow-up study, five researchers used LitPivot on their own ongoing projects during 30-minute sessions. Participants used LitPivot across multiple project phases, not just at the beginning. Two used it to vet new ideas against the literature, while three used it to refine the framing of more mature ideas. One researcher highlighted how seeing parallel concepts from different domains helped them reframe their contribution.
These studies suggest that LitPivot can support both early exploration and the refinement of an existing research direction.

At Ai2, we’re developing AI to help researchers formulate testable ideas and examine the evidence behind them. Asta supports that effort through theory generation from published findings (Theorizer), synthesis, and hypothesis generation and testing on data (AutoDiscovery), while HARPA generates promising hypotheses informed by emerging research trends. Scideator lets researchers recombine elements of prior work into new ideas and assess their novelty, and IdeaSynth supports iterative refinement with feedback grounded in the literature.

Our recent study, Old Ideas, Novel Problems, examines the limits of automated novelty evaluation, showing how small prompt changes can alter an AI judge’s verdict on the same ideas. LitPivot extends this line of work by making the choice of relevant literature part of the revision process. Researchers can change which papers they use to assess a proposal as their idea develops, then use critiques and supporting excerpts to decide how to revise it. The system connects those decisions across the proposal’s problem, contribution, and evaluation plan.
We hope insights from LitPivot help scientists build on existing knowledge and turn early ideas into new contributions to their fields.

cards.summary_cn: 【Hugging Face 官方动态】LitPivot：通过文学景观中的动态情境化发展研究思路
fulltext_cn: 遇到一篇新论文可以改变研究想法的轨迹。研究人员可能会发现有人已经解决了他们提出的贡献，或者在论文中发现了一个未解决的问题，从而激发了新的探究方向。
我们将这个过程称为文献发起的转向：通过阅读先前的工作促使研究方向发生变化。它将研究人员经常必须单独管理的两项活动联系起来：提出一个想法并决定用哪些文献来衡量它。
我们与宾夕法尼亚大学的合作者开发了 LitPivot，这是一个帮助研究人员导航这些枢纽的系统。 LitPivot 使用通过 Asta Paper Finder 检索到的论文，围绕正在编辑的提案部分组织文献，提供由选定研究摘录支持的批评，并提出研究人员可以接受、编辑或拒绝的修订建议。 LitPivot 旨在用于早期研究构思，但该想法可能会扩展到更长的写作任务（即撰写论文的引言部分）。
在一项由 17 名研究人员参与的研究中，领域专家认为使用 LitPivot 开发的研究想法比使用文本编辑器和 AI 聊天工具开发的研究想法更具有文献基础。参与者还认为他们修改后的研究想法更加新颖和有用，并报告对周围文献有了更深入的理解。
LitPivot 将在底特律举行的 UIST 2026 上展示。请阅读此处的论文。
研究思想通过与文献的接触而发展。在对四个已完成的计算机科学研究项目的会议记录进行分析时，我们在所有四个项目中确定了 21 个文献发起的支点。这些分为两种类型：将想法与现有工作区分开来建立想法的新颖性，以及将想法与现有工作结合起来以在其基础上继续发展。在我们确定其贡献之前，这个项目本身经历了两个关键时期。
这些变化可能很难驾驭。在一项形成性研究中，五名研究人员使用文本编辑器和标准搜索工具制定了提案。他们一边努力发展自己的想法，一边对照文献进行批判性评估。当一篇论文对某个想法的新颖性提出质疑时，他们希望得到有关如何修改它的具体建议，并得到先前工作的支持。这些发现形成了 LitPivot 的评估，它将文献支持的批评与修改某个想法的选定部分的具体建议结合起来。

在 LitPivot 中，研究人员首先在编辑器中编写一个简短的提案，并启用我们所说的方面突出显示，它将一个明确的想法分割成不同的方面（即问题、贡献和评估）。要检查建议的方面，研究人员单击草稿中的该部分。相邻小组根据所选方面对相关论文进行分组（例如，根据选择评估方面时使用的评估方法对论文进行分组）并突出显示最相关的组。研究人员选择论文，请求评估，并审查建议的修订以及支持批评的摘录。然后根据与修订方面的相关性对文献进行重新排序。
特别是，LitPivot 将研究想法分为问题、建议贡献和评估计划。每个方面都有自己的相关文献集和相关性排名。 LitPivot 将检索到的论文围绕正在编辑的方面进行分组，让研究人员选择系统应使用哪些论文来评估草稿。
除了 Prism 等科学写作环境和 Claude Code 等代理助手之外，LitPivot 还探索了一种用于开发早期研究想法的新工作流程：选择文献进行评估，使用证据对其进行修改，并随着想法的变化重新考虑哪些论文重要。它的论文组和相关的批评使提案的每个部分的这些步骤变得明确，而研究人员控制着草案和用于评估草案的证据。
对于问题陈述，LitPivot 会寻找问题存在的证据以及问题重要的原因。为了评估拟议的贡献，它将所选论文已经解决的内容与它们描述的局限性和未来工作进行比较，寻找剩余的差距。对于评估计划，它检查提议的测试是否解决了研究问题以及如何评估类似的工作。然后，系统建议重写并附加支持引用。
改变想法的一个方面可能会使另一个方面过时。 LitPivot 标记可能需要修订的段落，例如不再充分评估修订后的贡献的评估计划。研究人员可以接受、编辑或拒绝建议，并随着提案的进展请求新论文或刷新文献排名。
一位研究参与者的转述示例。
在我们的实验室研究中，17 名研究人员各自使用 LitPivot 开发了一个指定的想法，并使用基线工具（一个文本编辑器和一个用于询问有关选定论文的问题的 AI 工具）开发了另一个想法。两种情况都使用相同的论文集。两位领域专家不知道使用了哪个系统，他们根据一个标准对最终的提案进行评分：他们如何很好地使用相关文献来支持和证明该想法。使用 LitPivot 制定的提案获得了更高的评级。
同一项研究的参与者还表示，与基线相比，LitPivot 使他们对周围文献有更深入的了解，并且自我报告其想法的新颖性和实用性得到了更大的改善。领域专家还审查了参与者的想法，并评价使用 LitPivot 修改的想法明显更好地基于相关文献。
我们实验室研究的一位参与者首先提议生成一致的、真实的合成医疗记录。 LitPivot 将多次医院就诊的一致性视为所选文献中的潜在差距。参与者审查了摘要并删除了有关单次访问笔记的论文。经过另一次评估后，他们将提案范围缩小到检测多次访问记录中的矛盾。这个例子展示了修改一个想法和选择用于评估它的文献如何能够相互告知。
在一项后续研究中，五名研究人员在 30 分钟的会议中在他们自己正在进行的项目中使用了 LitPivot。参与者在多个项目阶段使用 LitPivot，而不仅仅是在开始时。两个人用它来根据文献审查新想法，而三个人用它来完善更成熟想法的框架。一位研究人员强调了看到来自不同领域的并行概念如何帮助他们重新构建自己的贡献。
这些研究表明 LitPivot 可以支持早期探索和现有研究方向的完善。

在 Ai2，我们正在开发人工智能来帮助研究人员提出可测试的想法并检查其背后的证据。 Asta 通过从已发表的研究结果（Theorizer）生成理论、综合、假设生成和数据测试（AutoDiscovery）来支持这一努力，而 HARPA 根据新兴研究趋势生成有希望的假设。 Scideator 允许研究人员将先前工作的元素重新组合成新的想法并评估其新颖性，而 IdeaSynth 支持基于文献的反馈进行迭代细化。
我们最近的研究《旧想法，新问题》探讨了自动新颖性评估的局限性，展示了微小的即时变化如何改变人工智能法官对相同想法的裁决。 LitPivot 通过将相关文献的选择作为修订过程的一部分来扩展这一工作范围。研究人员可以随着想法的发展而改变他们用来评估提案的论文，然后使用批评和支持摘录来决定如何修改它。该系统将这些决策与提案的问题、贡献和评估计划联系起来。
我们希望 LitPivot 的见解能够帮助科学家在现有知识的基础上发展并将早期想法转化为对其领域的新贡献。

cards.summary: 【Meta】Meta is delaying the enforcement of its new business terms after publishers raised concerns that they could allow the company to scrape news sites for AI training, as reported earlier by Fast Company.…
fulltext: Meta is delaying the enforcement of its new business terms after publishers raised concerns that they could allow the company to scrape news sites for AI training, as reported earlier by Fast Company. In a statement to The Verge, Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts says the terms will go into effect on November 20th “to allow more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not.”

The business terms, which were originally supposed to go into effect on October 30th, appeared to give Meta permission to freely scrape the new sites that use its platforms, while using the material for AI training. Though Meta updated these terms to remove language about “training” its products, legal experts argued the change is not enough to rule out the possibility.

The News/Media Alliance sent a letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg on Thursday, demanding that the company revise its business terms over concerns that they would cause “severe harm” to publishers. Digital advertisers and publishers in the European Union and the UK also urged regulators to force Meta to halt its new terms.

In response to this backlash, Meta is now delaying its new terms entirely. Roberts says the delay will give Meta more time to lay out “how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” referring to the file that signals to scrapers whether they can crawl a site.
